To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

progression of non-target lesions (ie, lesions not previously identified as target lesions) is the most common cause for radiologic progressive disease in patients with clear renal cell carcinoma, followed by new lesions and progression of target lesions.
in patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma, the most common cause of radiologic progression is based on non-target lesions and new lesions, not progression of target lesions.
in the context of the METEOR trial, the most common cause of radiologic progression of metastatic clear cell RCC was non-target disease and/or new lesions rather than progression of target lesions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of the most common causes of radiologic progression in patients with renal cell carcinoma.
the analysis of radiologic progression events in patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma.
the following: The most common cause of radiologic progressive renal cell carcinoma disease is not progression of existing target lesions but progression due to non–target disease and new lesions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the most common causes for progressive disease in the context of metastatic clear cell RCC were based on non-RECIST target lesions and new lesions rather then progression of the target lesions, and that these progression events were associated with a shorter median PFS.
progression of non-target lesions and new lesions are more common than progression of target lesions and that the former two have a negative impact on PFS.
the RECIST criteria are a useful and practical method for evaluating tumor response to treatment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

patients with metastatic RCC who experience radiologic progression due to non-RECIST 1 criteria (new lesions or non-target disease) have a significantly shorter PFS than those who experience RECIST-defined progression.
progression of renal cell cancer is more likely to be based on non-target and new lesions rather that change in target lesions.
the most common causes for progression in renal cell carcinoma were not due to the change in size of target lesions as defined by the Response Evaluation Criteria In Solid Tumors (RECIST) 1.1.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the most common cause of radiologic progression in metastatic renal cell carcinoma is not the change in target lesions.
the most common causes of progression in patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma are not the ones that are most often considered in the literature.
the most common causes for progression of disease are based on non-target lesions and new lesions rather then change in target lesions.
